title: Micro-organisms
standard_text: Micro-organisms include viruses, bacteria, protists and fungi. Some cause disease, while many are useful in food production, medicine and decomposition. The spread of disease can be reduced by hygiene and vaccination. (summary of CAPS Natural Sciences, Grade 8, Life and Living: Micro-organisms)
meta_desc: Free Grade 8 Natural Sciences worksheets (CAPS): viruses, bacteria, protists and fungi, harmful and useful micro-organisms, and preventing disease. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Most micro-organisms are harmless or useful.
key_sub: Hygiene and vaccines stop diseases spreading.
body_html:
How to think about it

Micro-organisms are living things too small to see without a microscope: bacteria, protists, some fungi (yeast) and viruses (which can only reproduce inside cells).

Some cause disease: tuberculosis (bacteria), HIV and flu (viruses), malaria (a protist) and thrush (a fungus). Many are useful: yeast in bread, bacteria in yoghurt and amasi, and decomposers in compost. Washing hands, clean water, vaccines and antibiotics (for bacteria) help to prevent and treat disease.

Example

Which micro-organism makes bread rise?

A fungus

Answer: yeast

Example

Can antibiotics cure flu?

Flu is caused by a virus.

Answer: no

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all micro-organisms are harmful.
  • Thinking antibiotics kill viruses.
  • Thinking viruses are cells.

items.q: A fungus makes potato plants rot (potato blight). Is this micro-organism helpful or harmful to people?
c: neither, because it is a plant
neither, because micro-organisms are not alive
items.e: Some micro-organisms help us; others cause illness or spoil food.

items.e: Making bread rise: yeast. (Yeast and moulds are both fungi.)

a thick yellow or green discharge and pain when urinating
flu-like illness, then damage to the immune system

flu-like illness, then damage to the immune system

items.e: Viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists.

items.q: Which measures help to prevent or control pneumococcal disease?
c: a yearly influenza vaccine, covering the nose and mouth when coughing, and washing hands
the pneumococcal vaccine and good hygiene; it is treated with antibiotics
items.e: Vaccination and hygiene reduce spread.

items.q: What causes pneumococcal disease?
items.e: Influenza is viral; pneumococcal disease is bacterial.

items.q: Which symptoms are typical of pneumococcal disease?
c: fever and chest pain; it can cause pneumonia, meningitis and blood infections
a red rash and itching only
fever, cough, sore throat, muscle aches and tiredness
items.e: Learn the main symptoms of each disease.

items.q: What type of pathogen causes pneumococcal disease?
items.e: Antibiotics can treat bacterial diseases, but not viral ones.

items.q: What type of pathogen causes dengue fever?
items.e: Antibiotics can treat bacterial diseases, but not viral ones.

items.q: Can dengue fever be treated with antibiotics?
c: only if a vaccine is also given
items.e: Dengue fever is caused by a virus. Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses.

items.q: Why does a vaccinated person not become ill when infected?
c: Memory cells make antibodies quickly, before the pathogen can multiply.
The vaccine kills all pathogens in the air.
The vaccine stays in the blood for ever as antibodies.
items.e: The secondary response is faster and larger.

items.q: Why should a patient finish the whole course of antibiotics?
c: to kill all the bacteria, so resistant ones are less likely to survive and multiply
items.e: Stopping early can leave the toughest bacteria alive.

items.q: What type of pathogen causes the common cold?
items.e: Antibiotics can treat bacterial diseases, but not viral ones.

items.q: How do antibiotic-resistant bacteria arise?
c: The patient becomes resistant to the antibiotic.
A random mutation makes some bacteria resistant; they survive the antibiotic and multiply.
items.e: This is natural selection.

items.q: Can tetanus be treated with antibiotics?
c: only if a vaccine is also given
items.e: Tetanus is caused by a bacterium. Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses.

items.q: What type of pathogen causes tetanus?
items.e: Antibiotics can treat bacterial diseases, but not viral ones.

items.q: How is pneumococcal disease mainly spread?
c: droplets from the nose and throat of an infected person
items.e: Both are spread by droplets from the airways.

items.q: How is influenza mainly spread?
c: droplets from coughs and sneezes, and touching contaminated surfaces
items.e: Both are spread by droplets from the airways.

items.q: Which measures help to prevent or control influenza?
c: the pneumococcal vaccine and good hygiene; it is treated with antibiotics
a yearly influenza vaccine, covering the nose and mouth when coughing, and washing hands
items.e: Vaccination and hygiene reduce spread.

items.q: What is herd immunity?
c: When most people are vaccinated, the disease cannot spread easily, protecting those who are not immune.
items.e: This protects babies and people who cannot be vaccinated.

items.q: What type of pathogen causes tuberculosis?
items.e: Antibiotics can treat bacterial diseases, but not viral ones.

items.q: Which cells make antibodies?
items.e: Phagocytes engulf pathogens.

items.q: Can cholera be treated with antibiotics?
c: only if a vaccine is also given
items.e: Cholera is caused by a bacterium. Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses.

items.q: What causes influenza?
items.e: Influenza is viral; pneumococcal disease is bacterial.

items.q: A nurse is given a booster dose of the tetanus vaccine. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: How do cilia in the trachea and bronchi help defend the body?
c: They attach to antigens on pathogens so they can be destroyed.
They move mucus with trapped pathogens up to the throat.
They neutralise toxins made by bacteria.
They trap particles that may contain pathogens.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: A newborn baby is protected for a few months by antibodies that crossed the placenta from its mother. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: How do bacteria make us ill?
c: They reproduce quickly and may make toxins that damage tissues.
items.e: Toxins.

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Kills pathogens in food and drink”?
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: Which is a way to reduce the spread of disease?
c: hand washing, vaccination and isolating infected people
items.e: Hygiene.

items.q: A person recovers from influenza and makes memory cells. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: How do antitoxins help defend the body?
c: They trap particles that may contain pathogens.
It acts as a barrier and makes antimicrobial secretions.
They neutralise toxins made by bacteria.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Engulf and digest pathogens”?
c: cilia in the trachea and bronchi
hairs and mucus in the nose
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: How do viruses make us ill?
c: They make toxins outside cells only.
They live and reproduce inside cells, damaging them.
items.e: Cell damage.

items.q: A fetus receives antibodies across the placenta. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: A traveller is given a hepatitis A vaccine before a trip. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: A patient with a dangerous infection is given a serum of antibodies from a donor. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: How do antibodies help defend the body?
c: They trap particles that may contain pathogens.
They move mucus with trapped pathogens up to the throat.
They attach to antigens on pathogens so they can be destroyed.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: A child is given the pneumococcal vaccine. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Move mucus with trapped pathogens up to the throat”?

cilia in the trachea and bronchi
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

They move mucus with trapped pathogens up to the throat.
They trap particles that may contain pathogens.
They neutralise toxins made by bacteria.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: What is a pathogen?
c: a type of white blood cell
items.e: Viruses, bacteria, fungi, protists.

items.q: A person bitten by a snake is given an injection of ready-made antibodies (antivenom). Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).
